# Overview

The **North Temperate Lakes Long-Term Ecological Research Program (NTL-LTER)** in Wisconsin has monitored fish populations since 1981 — one of the longest continuous fish datasets in North America. **Cisco** (*Coregonus artedi*) are especially important because they depend on cold, oxygen-rich water. As lakes warm with climate change, cisco are predicted to decline. Understanding how body size varies among years is one way biologists track whether populations are changing.

In Lectures 05–06 and 09–10 (Worksheets 05, 06, 09–10) you learned to wrangle data, calculate descriptive statistics, and run a two-sample Welch's t-test. This homework asks you to apply all those skills to a new, real dataset and answer: **Did cisco body weight differ between 1981 and 1982 in Trout Lake?**

### How to turn it in

**Submit to Canvas:** (1) your completed `.R` script, (2) three saved PNG figures (the two from Parts 1–6, plus the boxplot from Part 7), and (3) **one scanned or photographed page** with your handwritten answers to Parts 8 and 9. Fill in all Part 1–7 answer boxes **in the script as `#` comments** below the relevant code. The question numbers here match the `# Q__` markers in the skeleton script.

**Parts 8 and 9 must be answered by hand on paper**, photographed clearly, and uploaded as an image or embedded in your submission. Typed answers to those parts receive **at most half credit, even if correct** — I want to see your own handwriting and your own reasoning as you worked it out, not a pasted AI answer.

# The Data

| Column       | Type | What it holds                 |
|--------------|------|-------------------------------|
| `lakeid`     | chr  | lake code (`TR` = Trout Lake) |
| `year4`      | num  | year of catch (1981–2006)     |
| `sampledate` | chr  | sampling date (MM/DD/YYYY)    |
| `gearid`     | chr  | gill-net mesh size code       |
| `spname`     | chr  | species (always `CISCO`)      |
| `length`     | num  | total body length **(mm)**    |
| `weight`     | num  | body weight **(g)**           |
| `sex`        | chr  | M, F, I, or NA                |

**Source:** Ogle DH (2023). *FSAdata* R package / NTL-LTER, UW–Madison.

::: callout-note
Both groups may fail Shapiro-Wilk (p \< 0.05). With **n \> 80** the t-test is robust to non-normality because of the Central Limit Theorem — the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal even when raw data are not. Check the QQ plot: if points roughly follow the line without extreme curvature, proceed. (See Lecture 09, Step 2)
:::

# Going further (optional — no points)

Run the code below in your script to visualize the **full 25-year time series** of mean Cisco body weight. Does body size show a trend over the monitoring period?

``` r
cisco_raw_df %>%
  filter(!is.na(weight), weight > 0) %>%
  group_by(year4) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), mean_wt = mean(weight, na.rm = TRUE),
            se_wt = sd(weight, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year4, y = mean_wt)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), color = "darkblue", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(color = "darkblue", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_wt - se_wt, ymax = mean_wt + se_wt),
                width = 0.3, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed", color = "tomato") +
  labs(title = "25-Year Cisco Body Weight Trend — Trout Lake, WI",
       subtitle = "Annual mean ± SE; point size = sample size",
       x = "Year", y = "Mean Body Weight (g)",
       caption = "Dashed line = linear trend. NTL-LTER / FSAdata") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Compare the slope of that 25-year trend line to the 1981–1982 difference you just tested: a single year-to-year swing in mean weight can be as large as, or larger than, the change over the entire time series. That's a reminder to check whether two years you're comparing happen to sit on either side of unusual conditions (a warm summer, a strong year class) before reading too much into a two-year comparison alone.
